title: Diseases of the Special Senses
subject: Nervous System (NEUR)

overview.intro: This chapter covers the common diseases of the eye and ear: lid and conjunctival disease, the red eye, glaucoma, lens and retinal disorders, vascular loss of vision, refractive error and amblyopia, middle and outer ear infection, vertigo, hearing loss, orbital infection, and eye injury. Board items in this area are usually recognition questions built on one or two mechanistic clues, such as pain versus no pain, watery versus purulent discharge, sudden versus gradual loss, or vertigo lasting seconds, hours, or days. Each section explains where the clue comes from in the anatomy and physiology, so that an unfamiliar vignette can be reasoned through rather than memorized.
prerequisites: Anatomy of the eyelid, conjunctiva, cornea, uvea, lens, retina, and orbit
Aqueous humor production and drainage, and the autonomic control of the pupil and lens
Retinal layers, the retinal pigment epithelium, and the dual retinal and choroidal blood supply
Sound conduction through the outer and middle ear, cochlear hair cell transduction, and the vestibular labyrinth
Hypersensitivity types and the major pyogenic bacteria and herpesviruses

connections.how: S. aureus, Pseudomonas, the otitis media trio, N. gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, HSV, CMV, Toxoplasma, and Acanthamoeba each produce a characteristic eye or ear infection.
Aldose reductase explains diabetic and galactosemic cataract, and fibrillin and cystathionine beta-synthase explain ectopia lentis.
The retina is the only place where arterioles can be viewed directly, so hypertension, diabetes, and carotid atheroembolism leave readable signs there.
HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies, sarcoidosis, and juvenile idiopathic arthritis present with anterior uveitis, and AIDS permits CMV retinitis.
Papilledema, amblyopia, and the central versus peripheral vertigo distinction depend on optic nerve, visual cortex, and brainstem anatomy.

terms.def: Visible dilation of conjunctival or ciliary vessels, a shared sign of conjunctivitis, keratitis, uveitis, and angle-closure glaucoma.
A ring of injection at the limbus from dilated deep anterior ciliary vessels, signaling corneal or intraocular inflammation rather than conjunctivitis.
A layer of leukocytes settled in the inferior anterior chamber.
Enlargement of the central depression of the optic disc as retinal ganglion cell axons are lost.
Yellow extracellular deposits between the retinal pigment epithelium and Bruch membrane.
The potassium-rich fluid of the membranous labyrinth, secreted by the stria vascularis.
Calcium carbonate crystals on the utricular and saccular maculae that make those organs sensitive to gravity and linear acceleration.
Hearing loss caused by failure of sound to reach the cochlea through the canal, tympanic membrane, or ossicles.
Hearing loss caused by damage to cochlear hair cells, the cochlear nerve, or central auditory pathways.
A weaker pupillary response to light shone in one eye than in the other, indicating asymmetric retinal or optic nerve damage.

blocks.text: The eyelid margin carries three gland systems. Glands of Zeis are sebaceous glands opening into lash follicles, glands of Moll are apocrine sweat glands beside the lashes, and meibomian glands are long sebaceous glands embedded in the tarsal plate that secrete the lipid layer of the tear film. That lipid layer slows tear evaporation, so meibomian disease shows up as dryness and burning.

Blepharitis is chronic inflammation of the lid margin, and it is divided by location. Anterior blepharitis involves the lash base. Staphylococcal disease produces crusts and collarettes around the lashes, and seborrheic disease produces greasy scales, often with seborrheic dermatitis of the scalp and face. Posterior blepharitis is meibomian gland dysfunction: the glands secrete thick, turbid oil and their orifices plug, the tear film evaporates quickly, and the patient has gritty, burning, red eyes that are often worse in the morning. It is strongly associated with rosacea. Both forms are chronic, recurrent, and usually bilateral.

A hordeolum is an acute suppurative infection of a lid gland, usually by S. aureus. An external hordeolum (stye) involves a gland of Zeis or Moll and points at the lash line; an internal hordeolum involves a meibomian gland and points toward the conjunctiva. Acute neutrophilic inflammation makes it red, warm, and tender. A chalazion is different in kind: a blocked meibomian gland releases its lipid into the surrounding tarsus, and the lipid provokes a chronic sterile lipogranuloma with macrophages and giant cells. The result is a firm, painless nodule within the lid that develops over weeks. A chalazion may follow a hordeolum. A chalazion that keeps recurring in the same place in an older adult raises concern for sebaceous carcinoma, which can mimic it.

blocks.title: Lid margin lesions
rows: Acute bacterial infection, usually S. aureus
blocks.caption: Infection is acute and painful; retained lipid is granulomatous and painless.

blocks.text: The lens is transparent because its fibers have lost their nuclei and organelles and are packed with crystallin proteins arranged in a highly ordered, closely spaced array. The lens has no blood supply and lives on glucose and antioxidants from the aqueous humor, and its fibers are never shed, so the proteins must last for life. A cataract is any opacity of the lens. It forms when crystallins are oxidized, glycated, cross-linked, and aggregated into particles large enough to scatter light, or when fluid enters the fibers and disrupts their ordered packing.

Age is the dominant cause. Nuclear cataract yellows and hardens the central lens and raises its refractive index, which can produce a myopic shift. Cortical cataract forms spokes in the outer fibers and is linked to ultraviolet exposure. Posterior subcapsular cataract forms just under the back of the capsule and is typical of corticosteroid use, diabetes, and radiation. Smoking adds oxidative stress. Congenital rubella infects the developing lens and causes cataract together with sensorineural deafness and patent ductus arteriosus.

Diabetes and galactosemia share an osmotic mechanism. Aldose reductase in the lens reduces excess glucose to sorbitol and excess galactose to galactitol. The lens has little sorbitol dehydrogenase to oxidize sorbitol further, and galactitol cannot be metabolized at all, so these polyols accumulate, draw water into the fibers, and cause swelling and opacity. Infants with galactosemia (classic galactose 1-phosphate uridyltransferase deficiency or galactokinase deficiency) can develop cataracts in the first weeks of life.

Symptoms follow directly from scattering. Vision blurs slowly and painlessly, contrast falls, and glare and halos appear around lights, especially at night. The opacity blocks light returning from the fundus, so the red reflex dims or disappears. In an infant an absent red reflex or white pupil (leukocoria) must be distinguished from retinoblastoma.

blocks.title: Polyol pathway cataract
steps: High glucose or galactose enters lens fibers freely
Aldose reductase forms sorbitol or galactitol
Polyol cannot be cleared efficiently and is trapped

Fiber disruption and protein aggregation scatter light
Painless blurred vision, glare, loss of red reflex
blocks.caption: The same osmotic pathway explains diabetic and galactosemic cataract.

blocks.text: The conjunctiva is a mucous membrane lining the inner lids and covering the sclera up to the limbus. When inflamed, its superficial vessels dilate most in the fornices and fade toward the cornea, vision stays normal, and the pupil reacts normally, which separates conjunctivitis from the more dangerous red eyes in the next sections. The type of discharge and the type of conjunctival reaction point to the cause. Follicles are lymphoid aggregates and suggest viral or chlamydial infection; papillae are swellings with a central vascular core and suggest bacterial or allergic disease.

Viral conjunctivitis is most often adenovirus. It produces a watery discharge, follicles, a tender preauricular lymph node, and often spreads to the second eye within days. It is highly contagious through hands and instruments; some serotypes cause epidemic keratoconjunctivitis and others pharyngoconjunctival fever. Bacterial conjunctivitis (S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, Moraxella) produces purulent discharge that glues the lids shut in the morning. Neisseria gonorrhoeae causes hyperacute conjunctivitis with copious pus and lid swelling; it can invade intact corneal epithelium and perforate the cornea within days, which makes it an emergency.

Chlamydia trachomatis serovars D to K cause adult inclusion conjunctivitis, a chronic follicular conjunctivitis transmitted sexually or from genital secretions, often with urethritis or cervicitis. Serovars A to C cause trachoma, spread by hands, flies, and shared cloths in areas with poor water access. Repeated infection scars the upper tarsal conjunctiva, the scar contracts and turns the lid inward (entropion), lashes rub the cornea (trichiasis), and corneal scarring follows. Trachoma is the leading infectious cause of blindness worldwide. In neonates, gonococcal conjunctivitis typically appears at 2 to 5 days and chlamydial at about 5 to 14 days.

Allergic conjunctivitis is a type I hypersensitivity reaction: allergen cross-links IgE on conjunctival mast cells, and histamine causes itching, vasodilation, and chemosis (conjunctival edema). Itching is the most specific symptom, the discharge is watery or stringy, and both eyes are affected, often with allergic rhinitis.

blocks.title: Distinguishing conjunctivitis
rows: Follicles, preauricular node, recent URI, spreads to other eye
Marked lid swelling, risk of corneal perforation
blocks.caption: Discharge, follicles versus papillae, and itching identify the cause.

blocks.text: Aqueous humor is secreted by the nonpigmented ciliary epithelium into the posterior chamber, a process that depends on carbonic anhydrase and Na+/K+ ATPase. It flows through the pupil into the anterior chamber and leaves mainly through the trabecular meshwork in the angle between iris and cornea, then through the canal of Schlemm into episcleral veins; a smaller fraction leaves by the uveoscleral route. Intraocular pressure (IOP) reflects the balance between production and outflow resistance, and the normal range is about 10 to 21 mmHg.

Glaucoma is an optic neuropathy, not simply high pressure. Retinal ganglion cell axons are lost where they bend through the lamina cribrosa at the optic disc, so the central cup of the disc enlarges (a cup-to-disc ratio above about 0.6, or asymmetry between eyes, is suspicious) and the rim thins. Raised IOP is the main modifiable risk factor, but glaucoma can occur at normal pressure, and some eyes tolerate high pressure without damage. Arcuate nerve fiber bundles are lost first, so visual field loss begins in the periphery and central acuity is spared until late.

Primary open-angle glaucoma is the common form. The angle looks open, but outflow resistance in the trabecular meshwork rises, IOP climbs slowly, and the patient notices nothing until much of the peripheral field is gone. Risk rises with age, African ancestry, family history, and myopia. Acute angle-closure glaucoma is mechanically different. In a small hyperopic eye with a shallow anterior chamber and an enlarging lens, the iris presses against the lens and blocks flow through the pupil (pupillary block). Pressure builds behind the iris, bows it forward, and the peripheral iris seals the trabecular meshwork. Mid-dilation of the pupil, as in dim light or with an anticholinergic or sympathomimetic drug, maximizes iris-lens contact and slackens the peripheral iris, which is why it triggers attacks.

In an attack, IOP rises abruptly, often above 40 mmHg. Pressure forces water into the corneal epithelium, and the edematous cornea looks hazy and diffracts light into halos around lights. Severe pain and headache arise from the trigeminal nerve, and nausea and vomiting are reflex vagal effects. Ischemia of the iris sphincter leaves the pupil fixed and mid-dilated, the eye is red with ciliary flush, and the globe feels hard.

blocks.title: Acute angle closure
steps: Shallow anterior chamber in a hyperopic, older eye
Pupil mid-dilates in dim light or with drugs
Iris-lens contact blocks aqueous flow through pupil
Iris bows forward and seals trabecular meshwork
Outflow stops and IOP rises sharply
Corneal edema, halos, pain, vomiting, fixed mid-dilated pupil
blocks.caption: Pupillary block converts normal aqueous production into a pressure emergency.

blocks.title: Open-angle versus acute angle-closure glaucoma
rows: Blurring with halos, rapid loss if untreated
blocks.caption: Both end in optic nerve damage, by very different routes.

blocks.predict: Why can a patient with open-angle glaucoma have 20/20 vision while losing a large part of the visual field?
blocks.explain: Ganglion cell axons from the arcuate bundles above and below the fovea are lost first, while the papillomacular bundle that carries central vision is preserved until late. Acuity tests the fovea only.
blocks.check: The paragraph on optic neuropathy and field loss.

blocks.text: The cornea is avascular and has the densest sensory innervation in the body (trigeminal V1), so corneal disease causes pain, tearing, photophobia, and a foreign body sensation, and it threatens vision because any scar lies in the visual axis. Keratitis is corneal inflammation, and an ulcer is an epithelial defect with an underlying stromal infiltrate. Risks for ulcer include contact lens wear (hypoxia, microtrauma, and organisms carried on the lens or in its case), trauma, dry eye, poor lid closure, and topical steroid use.

Herpes simplex virus (usually HSV-1) reactivates from the trigeminal ganglion and infects corneal epithelium. Infected cells die and slough in a branching line, the dendritic ulcer, which stains with fluorescein and ends in small terminal bulbs. Viral damage to corneal nerves reduces corneal sensation. Recurrences can involve the stroma, where immune inflammation causes scarring, so HSV is a leading infectious cause of corneal blindness in developed countries. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is the classic contact lens organism: it adheres to damaged epithelium, secretes proteases, and can produce a rapidly enlarging ulcer with stromal melting and perforation. Acanthamoeba is a free-living amoeba in tap water, pools, and hot tubs; infection follows rinsing lenses in tap water or swimming in them. It causes pain out of proportion to the findings, a ring infiltrate, and inflammation along corneal nerves, and its cysts are very resistant.

Anterior uveitis (iritis or iridocyclitis) is inflammation of the iris and ciliary body. The injection is a ciliary flush concentrated at the limbus. Inflammation breaks the blood-aqueous barrier, so protein and cells leak into the anterior chamber and are seen on slit lamp as flare and cells, and leukocytes may deposit on the corneal endothelium (keratic precipitates) or layer as a hypopyon. The inflamed iris sphincter goes into spasm, making the pupil small, and sticky exudate glues the iris to the lens (posterior synechiae), making it irregular when it later dilates. Light causes pain because constriction of the inflamed iris and ciliary muscle hurts; this pain occurs even when light is shone in the opposite eye, through the consensual reflex.

blocks.title: The red eye
blocks.caption: Pain, reduced vision, an abnormal pupil, or a corneal change mark a red eye as more than conjunctivitis.

blocks.text: The macula, and the fovea at its center, are packed with cones and provide central, high-acuity, color vision. Photoreceptors depend on the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), which recycles visual pigment, phagocytoses shed outer segment discs, and transports nutrients from the choriocapillaris across Bruch membrane. Each RPE cell digests an enormous load of lipid-rich membrane over a lifetime, and incompletely digested material accumulates.

Age-related macular degeneration (AMD) is the leading cause of irreversible central vision loss in older adults in developed countries. Risk factors are age (usually over 50), smoking, family history, and variants in complement genes such as complement factor H, which point to chronic complement-mediated injury at Bruch membrane. Oxidative stress, including that from smoking, adds to it.

Dry (nonexudative) AMD is about 85 to 90% of cases. Drusen, yellow deposits of lipid, protein, and complement components, collect between the RPE basal lamina and Bruch membrane and impair exchange between the choroid and the outer retina. The RPE and overlying photoreceptors gradually atrophy, ending in sharply bordered patches of geographic atrophy. Central vision fades slowly over years, with difficulty reading and recognizing faces.

Wet (neovascular or exudative) AMD is less common but causes most severe vision loss. Stressed and hypoxic RPE releases vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF), and new vessels grow from the choroid through breaks in Bruch membrane beneath the RPE or retina (choroidal neovascularization). These vessels are fragile and leaky, so fluid and blood collect under the macula within days to weeks. Photoreceptors displaced by fluid make straight lines look bent (metamorphopsia), a central dark spot appears, and untreated lesions organize into a fibrovascular scar. In both forms the peripheral retina is spared, so patients keep navigational vision. Dry AMD can convert to wet AMD, which is why sudden distortion in a patient with drusen is significant.

rows: Chronic RPE and Bruch membrane injury
blocks.caption: VEGF-driven leakage makes wet AMD fast.

blocks.text: The uvea (iris, ciliary body, and choroid) is highly vascular, so it is a frequent site of immune-mediated and hematogenous disease. Uveitis is classified anatomically: anterior uveitis involves the iris and ciliary body and presents as a painful red eye with photophobia; posterior uveitis involves the choroid and retina and presents as painless floaters and blurred vision, because the iris and ciliary muscle, whose spasm causes the pain and photophobia, are spared, and inflammatory cells in the vitreous cast shadows on the retina. Knowing the location narrows the systemic cause.

Acute anterior uveitis is the most common extra-articular feature of the HLA-B27 spondyloarthropathies: ankylosing spondylitis, reactive arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and the arthritis of inflammatory bowel disease. Attacks are sudden, usually unilateral, and recurrent, and may alternate between eyes, often with a fibrinous exudate or hypopyon. Sarcoidosis causes granulomatous uveitis, often bilateral and chronic, with large greasy keratic precipitates made of epithelioid macrophages; it can involve the anterior or posterior segment and also the lacrimal glands. Juvenile idiopathic arthritis, particularly the oligoarticular form in young ANA-positive girls, causes chronic anterior uveitis that is quiet: the eye is white and painless, so cataract, glaucoma, and band keratopathy can develop before anyone notices.

Toxoplasma gondii is the most common cause of infectious posterior uveitis in immunocompetent people. Tissue cysts in the retina, often from congenital infection, reactivate at the edge of an old pigmented scar and produce a focus of necrotizing retinochoroiditis with overlying vitritis, which looks like a headlight in fog. Cytomegalovirus retinitis occurs in advanced AIDS, typically with a CD4 count below 50 cells per microliter. Without cell-mediated immunity, the virus spreads cell to cell through the retina, producing yellow-white necrosis with hemorrhage along vessels and little vitreous inflammation because there are too few T cells to mount it. It is painless, progresses relentlessly, and can cause retinal detachment.

rows: Retinochoroiditis beside old scar, dense vitritis

blocks.caption: Location and tempo of the uveitis point to the systemic disease.

blocks.text: The membranous labyrinth is filled with endolymph, an unusual extracellular fluid with a high potassium concentration (about 150 mmol/L) and low sodium. Endolymph is secreted in the cochlea by the stria vascularis and resorbed largely by the endolymphatic sac. When transduction channels open, potassium flows from endolymph into hair cells, driven mainly by the electrical gradient (in the cochlea, the endocochlear potential of about +80 mV), so the volume and composition of endolymph must be held tightly.

Meniere disease is idiopathic endolymphatic hydrops: excess endolymph distends the cochlear duct and vestibular compartments, most likely because resorption by the endolymphatic sac is impaired. Reissner membrane bulges into the scala vestibuli. Episodes are thought to occur when distension or small ruptures let potassium-rich endolymph mix with perilymph, which first depolarizes and then temporarily silences hair cells and nerve endings. While the vestibular input from one ear is abnormal, the brain perceives rotation, so the patient has violent spinning vertigo with nausea, vomiting, and nystagmus.

The clinical pattern follows from this mechanism. Attacks of vertigo last from about 20 minutes to 12 hours, longer than BPPV and shorter than vestibular neuritis. Hearing loss is sensorineural and fluctuating, and it affects low frequencies first, probably because the apex of the cochlea, which encodes low frequencies, has the widest and most compliant basilar membrane and is the first region distorted by excess volume. Tinnitus is typically low-pitched and roaring, and a sense of fullness or pressure in the ear reflects distension. Early in the disease hearing recovers between attacks; with repeated episodes hair cells are lost, and hearing loss becomes permanent and extends across frequencies. Most cases are unilateral at onset.

blocks.title: The Meniere tetrad
rows: Episodic vertigo, about 20 minutes to 12 hours
Asymmetric vestibular hair cell firing during the attack
Hydrops thought to distort the compliant cochlear apex first
blocks.caption: Each element of the tetrad traces to hydrops.

blocks.text: The middle ear is an air-filled space whose only connection to the outside is the eustachian tube, which opens during swallowing through contraction of the tensor veli palatini. The tube ventilates the middle ear, drains its secretions into the nasopharynx, and protects it from nasopharyngeal contents. In young children the tube is shorter, more horizontal, and floppier, and adenoid tissue sits near its opening, so it obstructs easily. Children with cleft palate or Down syndrome have particularly poor tube function.

Acute otitis media (AOM) usually follows a viral upper respiratory infection. Mucosal swelling closes the tube, the trapped middle ear gas is absorbed into the blood, and pressure in the middle ear falls. Negative pressure draws in transudate and nasopharyngeal secretions, and bacteria colonizing the nasopharynx multiply in the static fluid. The three main pathogens are Streptococcus pneumoniae, nontypeable Haemophilus influenzae (unencapsulated, so not covered by the Hib vaccine), and Moraxella catarrhalis. Pus under pressure produces ear pain, fever, irritability, and a red, bulging, immobile tympanic membrane.

Otitis media with effusion (OME) is fluid in the middle ear without signs of acute infection. It often follows AOM or persistent tube dysfunction. The membrane is dull, retracted or neutral, and moves poorly, sometimes with an air-fluid level. Because fluid damps the vibration of the membrane and ossicles, OME causes conductive hearing loss, and persistent loss in a young child can delay speech and language.

Complications follow the anatomy. Pressure can rupture the membrane (perforation), which relieves pain and releases discharge. The middle ear connects with the mastoid air cells through the aditus and antrum, so infection can spread there; mastoiditis causes postauricular pain and swelling that pushes the auricle forward and outward. Chronic negative pressure can draw a pocket of the membrane inward, and keratinizing squamous epithelium trapped in the pocket grows into a cholesteatoma, a collection of keratin that erodes bone, including the ossicles. Cholesteatoma causes painless, foul-smelling discharge and conductive loss, and it can reach the facial nerve, labyrinth, or cranial cavity. Spread to meninges, brain, or the sigmoid sinus is rare but serious.

blocks.title: Pathogenesis of acute otitis media
steps: Viral URI swells nasopharynx and eustachian tube
Tube closes and middle ear gas is absorbed

Nasopharyngeal bacteria multiply in trapped fluid
Pus under pressure: pain, fever, bulging membrane
blocks.caption: Tube dysfunction comes first; infection exploits the trapped fluid.

blocks.predict: Why does a child with acute otitis media often have sudden relief of pain followed by ear discharge?
blocks.explain: Pus under pressure stretches the pain-sensitive tympanic membrane. When the membrane perforates, pressure falls at once and the pus drains into the canal.

blocks.text: The external canal is lined by skin. Its outer third rests on cartilage and contains hair follicles and ceruminous glands; its inner two thirds lies on bone. Cerumen is acidic and water-repellent and contains antimicrobial lipids and peptides, so it protects the canal skin. Moisture from swimming, humidity, or sweating removes cerumen and macerates the skin, and scratching or cotton swabs break the barrier. That combination permits otitis externa (swimmer's ear), usually caused by Pseudomonas aeruginosa or Staphylococcus aureus, and less often by fungi such as Aspergillus.

The canal skin is tightly bound to the underlying perichondrium and periosteum, so even small amounts of swelling stretch sensitive tissue. Pain on pressing the tragus or pulling the auricle is therefore the characteristic sign, and it helps separate otitis externa from otitis media. The canal is swollen and red with discharge, and conductive hearing loss occurs when the canal closes.

Malignant (necrotizing) otitis externa is a Pseudomonas osteomyelitis of the temporal bone and skull base. It occurs mainly in older adults with diabetes, whose microangiopathy and impaired neutrophil function allow infection to spread through fissures in the cartilaginous canal and into bone. Severe, persistent, often nocturnal pain and granulation tissue on the floor of the canal at the bony-cartilaginous junction are typical. As infection spreads medially it involves cranial nerves at their foramina: the facial nerve at the stylomastoid foramen is affected first and most often, and further spread reaches the jugular foramen (IX, X, XI) and hypoglossal canal (XII). The inflammatory markers are elevated, and the disease can be fatal.

Auricular perichondritis is infection of the perichondrium of the ear cartilage. Cartilage has no blood vessels and depends on diffusion from the perichondrium, so when pus separates the two, cartilage necroses and can collapse into a deformed ear. Piercing through the upper ear cartilage is a classic route, and Pseudomonas is the usual organism. The ear is red, hot, and tender, but the lobule is spared because it contains no cartilage.

blocks.text: At rest, the vestibular nerves on both sides fire at equal tonic rates, and the brain reads the difference between the sides as head rotation. Any sudden one-sided loss of input mimics a turn toward the healthy side, causing vertigo and a horizontal-torsional nystagmus whose slow phase drifts toward the damaged ear and whose fast phase beats away from it. The duration of vertigo and whether hearing is affected identify the peripheral cause.

Vestibular neuritis is inflammation of the vestibular nerve, presumed viral (reactivated HSV-1 is suspected), usually involving the superior division. The patient has sudden, continuous, severe vertigo with nausea and vomiting lasting days, then gradual improvement over weeks as the brain recalibrates. Hearing is normal because the cochlear nerve is spared. The head impulse test shows a corrective saccade when the head is turned quickly toward the affected side, because the vestibulo-ocular reflex on that side fails, and the patient tends to fall toward the affected side. Labyrinthitis is inflammation of the labyrinth itself, including the cochlea, so the same vertigo is accompanied by sensorineural hearing loss and tinnitus. An acute continuous vertigo can also be a cerebellar or brainstem stroke; a normal head impulse test, nystagmus that changes direction with gaze, a vertical skew deviation, or inability to stand points to a central cause.

Benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV) is the most common cause of vertigo. Otoconia detach from the utricular macula, often with aging or head trauma, and drift into a semicircular canal, most often the posterior canal because it is the most dependent when the person is upright or lying. When the head moves in the plane of that canal, the loose particles sink, drag endolymph, and deflect the cupula, so a canal that should sense only rotation now responds to gravity. Vertigo starts a few seconds after the position change, lasts less than a minute, and fades with repetition. The Dix-Hallpike maneuver reproduces it with an upbeating, torsional nystagmus. Hearing is normal.

blocks.text: The retina has two blood supplies. The central retinal artery, a branch of the ophthalmic artery (the first major branch of the internal carotid), enters through the optic nerve and supplies the inner retina, including the ganglion cells. The choroid supplies the outer retina, including the photoreceptors. The central retinal artery is an end artery, so its occlusion leaves the inner retina with no collateral flow.

Central retinal artery occlusion (CRAO) causes sudden, painless, severe monocular vision loss. Most cases are embolic, usually cholesterol or platelet-fibrin emboli from carotid atherosclerosis or emboli from the heart; giant cell arteritis is an important nonembolic cause in older adults. The ischemic inner retina becomes edematous and opaque, so the fundus looks pale white. The fovea has no inner retinal layers, so it stays thin and transparent, and the normal red of the underlying choroid shows through as a cherry-red spot. Arterioles are narrowed, the blood column may break into segments, and there is a relative afferent pupillary defect.

Amaurosis fugax is transient monocular vision loss, often described as a curtain coming down, lasting minutes and then clearing. It is usually caused by small emboli from an ipsilateral internal carotid plaque passing through retinal arterioles, and a bright refractile cholesterol embolus (Hollenhorst plaque) may be seen at an arteriolar branch. It is a retinal transient ischemic attack and signals a raised risk of stroke.

Central retinal vein occlusion (CRVO) is thrombosis of the central retinal vein, usually at the lamina cribrosa, where the artery and vein share an adventitial sheath and a stiff atherosclerotic artery can compress the vein. Risks include age, hypertension, diabetes, glaucoma, and hypercoagulable states. Blood still enters but cannot leave, so veins become dilated and tortuous, and hemorrhages spread through all four quadrants with disc swelling and cotton wool spots. Vision loss is painless but usually less abrupt and less complete than in CRAO. Ischemic CRVO drives VEGF release, which can cause iris neovascularization and neovascular glaucoma weeks to months later.

blocks.title: Painless monocular vision loss from vascular disease
rows: Venous thrombosis at the lamina cribrosa
Pale retina, cherry-red spot, narrow arterioles
Diffuse hemorrhages, dilated tortuous veins, disc swelling
Stroke equivalent; consider giant cell arteritis
blocks.caption: Arterial occlusion empties the retina; venous occlusion floods it.

blocks.title: Pale retina or bloody retina
blocks.text: A 72-year-old with hypertension wakes with painless loss of vision in the right eye. If the fundus is pale with a cherry-red spot, arterial inflow has stopped: the inner retina is ischemic, the fovea lets the choroid show through, and the likely sources are a carotid or cardiac embolus or giant cell arteritis, so jaw claudication or scalp tenderness matter. If instead the fundus shows hemorrhages in every quadrant with engorged veins, outflow is blocked and the arteries are still delivering blood into a congested retina. One lesion is upstream of the capillaries and the other downstream, so the same symptom gives opposite fundus pictures.

sections.title: Hypertensive and diabetic retinopathy and papilledema

blocks.text: Flame hemorrhages lie in the superficial nerve fiber layer, where blood spreads along the axons; dot and blot hemorrhages lie deeper, where cells are packed vertically. Cotton wool spots are microinfarcts of the nerve fiber layer in which axoplasmic transport stops and organelles accumulate in swollen axons. Hard exudates are yellow deposits of lipid and protein that leaked from abnormal capillaries.

In hypertensive retinopathy, retinal arterioles first constrict (autoregulatory narrowing) and then thicken by hyaline arteriolosclerosis, so the light reflex widens (copper or silver wiring). Where a thickened arteriole crosses a vein within their shared sheath, it compresses the vein (arteriovenous nicking). Severe pressure breaks down the blood-retina barrier, producing flame hemorrhages, cotton wool spots, and hard exudates, sometimes in a star around the macula. Swelling of the optic disc marks malignant hypertension.

In diabetic retinopathy, chronic hyperglycemia damages capillaries through advanced glycation end products, the polyol pathway, and oxidative stress. Pericytes are lost and basement membranes thicken. The weakened capillary wall balloons into microaneurysms, the earliest visible sign, and leaks to form dot and blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, and macular edema (nonproliferative retinopathy). Capillary closure makes the retina ischemic, and ischemic retina releases VEGF, which drives new vessels on the disc or retinal surface (proliferative retinopathy). These vessels bleed into the vitreous and pull on the retina as they scar, causing tractional detachment.

Papilledema is optic disc swelling caused by raised intracranial pressure. The subarachnoid space extends along the optic nerve sheath, so CSF pressure is transmitted to the nerve behind the eye, compresses it, and blocks axoplasmic flow at the lamina cribrosa. Axons swell, the disc margins blur and elevate, veins engorge, spontaneous venous pulsations are lost (though some normal people lack them), and the blind spot enlarges. It is usually bilateral, and acuity is preserved early, which separates it from optic neuritis, where vision falls early.

blocks.predict: Why do cotton wool spots appear in hypertension, diabetes, and CRVO alike?
blocks.explain: Each condition can cut off capillary flow to the nerve fiber layer (arteriolar damage in hypertension and diabetes, stagnant venous flow in CRVO), and the ischemic axons stop axoplasmic transport and swell with accumulated material.

blocks.text: The neurosensory retina is held against the RPE only loosely, by the pump function of the RPE and the matrix between photoreceptor outer segments. The two layers are the remnants of the two walls of the embryonic optic cup, and the potential space between them reopens in retinal detachment. Detached photoreceptors are separated from the choroid, which nourishes them, and they begin to degenerate.

Rhegmatogenous detachment, the common form, starts with a retinal tear. With age the vitreous liquefies and separates from the retina (posterior vitreous detachment), and where it remains firmly attached, it pulls a tear in the retina. Liquid vitreous then passes through the tear and lifts the retina off the RPE. Traction on the retina stimulates photoreceptors mechanically, which the patient sees as flashes (photopsia). Pigment and blood released into the vitreous cast shadows as a shower of floaters. As fluid spreads, a shadow or curtain advances over the visual field opposite the detached area, and central vision fails when the macula detaches. Myopia is a major risk because the elongated eye has a thin, stretched peripheral retina, often with lattice degeneration. Other risks are cataract surgery, trauma, and Marfan syndrome. Tractional detachment follows fibrovascular scarring in proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and exudative detachment follows fluid leakage from inflammation or tumor.

Retinitis pigmentosa is a group of inherited degenerations of photoreceptors and RPE with autosomal dominant, autosomal recessive, and X-linked forms; rhodopsin mutations are a common dominant cause. Rods are lost first, so the first symptom is night blindness, followed by loss of the midperipheral field that narrows to tunnel vision. Cones fail later, and central vision is lost last. As photoreceptors die, RPE cells migrate into the retina around vessels and form bone spicule pigment, the arterioles narrow, and the optic disc becomes waxy and pale. It can occur with sensorineural deafness in Usher syndrome and with vitamin A and E deficiency in abetalipoproteinemia.

blocks.text: The eye focuses light with about 60 diopters of total power. The cornea supplies about two thirds of it (roughly 43 diopters) and the lens about one third, and only the lens can change its power. To focus on a near object, the ciliary muscle contracts under parasympathetic control (oculomotor nerve, muscarinic receptors). Contraction moves the ciliary ring inward, slackens the zonular fibers, and lets the elastic capsule round up the lens, increasing its power. This is accommodation. Emmetropia means parallel light from a distant object focuses on the retina with accommodation relaxed.

In myopia the eye is too long for its optical power (or, less often, the cornea or lens is too strong), so distant images focus in front of the retina and far vision blurs while near vision stays clear. Diverging (minus) lenses neutralize it. In hyperopia the eye is too short, so images focus behind the retina. A young hyperopic eye can pull the image forward by accommodating, at the cost of eye strain, and converging (plus) lenses neutralize it. In astigmatism the cornea (or lens) is curved more steeply in one meridian than the other, like the back of a spoon, so no single point focus forms and vision blurs at all distances; cylindrical lenses neutralize it. Presbyopia is the age-related loss of accommodation: the lens keeps adding fibers, becomes larger and stiffer, and no longer rounds up when the zonules slacken. The near point recedes, and reading becomes difficult, usually from the early to mid forties.

Strabismus is misalignment of the eyes, inward (esotropia) or outward (exotropia). In adults new strabismus causes double vision. In a young child, whose visual cortex is still being wired during a critical period, the cortex instead suppresses the image from the deviating eye. Its inputs then lose competitive ground in the ocular dominance columns of primary visual cortex, and the eye becomes amblyopic: vision is reduced although the eye itself is normal. Unequal refractive error between the eyes (anisometropia) and a congenital cataract or ptosis that blocks the image cause amblyopia the same way. Hyperopia links the two topics: a hyperopic child who accommodates hard also converges, through the near reflex, and can develop accommodative esotropia. Because cortical wiring becomes fixed after early childhood, amblyopia that is not corrected early can become permanent.

rows: Eye too long or too powerful
Eye too short or too weak
blocks.caption: Myopia and hyperopia are mismatches between length and power; presbyopia is loss of accommodation.

blocks.text: Sound in air must enter the fluid-filled cochlea, and most of its energy would reflect at an air-fluid interface. The middle ear matches impedance: the tympanic membrane has about 17 to 20 times the area of the stapes footplate, and the ossicular lever adds a little more, so pressure at the oval window increases about 20-fold (roughly 25 to 30 dB). The basilar membrane is tuned by place, high frequencies at the base and low at the apex.

Conductive hearing loss occurs anywhere from the canal to the footplate. Cerumen impaction and otitis externa block the canal. A perforated tympanic membrane loses area and the pressure gain. Middle ear effusion and eustachian tube dysfunction damp the membrane and ossicles. In barotrauma, during a plane descent or a dive, outside pressure rises faster than a blocked tube can equalize, so the membrane is pushed inward and blood or fluid may enter the middle ear. Otosclerosis is abnormal remodeling of the otic capsule in which new spongy bone forms in front of the oval window and fixes the stapes footplate; it is often familial, more common in women, begins in young adults, and may worsen in pregnancy. The tympanic membrane looks normal. Cholesteatoma erodes the ossicles.

Sensorineural loss arises in the cochlea or the nerve. Presbycusis is gradual, bilateral, symmetric loss beginning at high frequencies, because hair cells at the basal turn are lost first; speech becomes hard to follow in noisy rooms. Noise damages outer hair cells mechanically and metabolically and typically produces a notch near 4 kHz on the audiogram. Tinnitus accompanies both types of loss. When cochlear input falls, neurons in the central auditory pathway raise their gain and fire spontaneously, which is heard as sound.

blocks.title: Tuning fork tests
rows: Air louder than bone, both reduced
blocks.caption: Weber lateralizes toward a conductive loss and away from a sensorineural loss.

blocks.title: Reading Weber and Rinne
blocks.text: A 30-year-old woman has gradual hearing loss in the left ear that worsened during pregnancy; the eardrums look normal. Weber is louder in the left ear. That alone could mean left conductive loss or right sensorineural loss. Rinne on the left is negative: she hears the fork better on the mastoid than in front of the canal, so air conduction is impaired and the cochlea is working. Rinne on the right is normal. The loss is conductive on the left. A conductive ear lateralizes Weber because room noise no longer masks bone-conducted sound and sound energy escapes less through the blocked path. A normal membrane, young female patient, and worsening in pregnancy point to otosclerosis fixing the stapes.

The orbital septum is a fibrous sheet running from the bony orbital rim to the tarsal plates. It divides the eyelid tissues in front from the orbital fat, muscles, and optic nerve behind, and it is a barrier to spread of infection. The medial orbital wall is the lamina papyracea, a paper-thin plate of the ethmoid bone, and the orbital veins communicate without valves with the facial veins, the sinuses, and the cavernous sinus.

Preseptal (periorbital) cellulitis is infection in front of the septum, usually after skin trauma, an insect bite, or a hordeolum, sometimes from sinusitis. The lids are red and swollen, but because the orbit is spared, vision, pupils, and eye movements are normal and there is no proptosis. Orbital cellulitis lies behind the septum and most often spreads from ethmoid sinusitis through the lamina papyracea, typically in children. Inflamed orbital contents cause pain with eye movement, proptosis, restricted movement (ophthalmoplegia), chemosis, and fever, and pressure on the optic nerve reduces vision and produces an afferent pupillary defect. Organisms include S. aureus, streptococci, and anaerobes; in diabetic ketoacidosis, mucormycosis must be considered. Complications are subperiosteal or orbital abscess, cavernous sinus thrombosis through the valveless veins, and meningitis.

Dacryocystitis is infection of the lacrimal sac. Tears drain through the puncta and canaliculi into the sac and down the nasolacrimal duct to the inferior meatus. Obstruction of the duct, congenital in infants (an imperforate membrane at its lower end) or acquired in older adults, causes stasis and infection, usually by S. aureus or streptococci. A tender red swelling appears at the inner corner of the eye below the medial canthal tendon, and pressure may express pus from the punctum.

Endophthalmitis is infection of the vitreous and aqueous inside the globe. Exogenous cases follow intraocular surgery such as cataract extraction (often coagulase-negative staphylococci from the patient's own lid flora) or penetrating trauma (Bacillus cereus is notoriously destructive). Endogenous cases come from bacteremia or fungemia, as with Candida in people with central lines or who inject drugs. Pain, rapidly falling vision, a hypopyon, and hazy vitreous develop, and the eye can be lost within days.

blocks.caption: Signs that come from orbital contents (motility, proptosis, vision) mean infection is behind the septum.

blocks.text: A pterygium is a triangular, wing-shaped growth of fibrovascular conjunctival tissue that extends from the bulbar conjunctiva across the limbus onto the cornea, usually on the nasal side. It is linked to chronic ultraviolet exposure, as in people who work outdoors in sunny, dry, dusty climates. Ultraviolet light damages limbal cells and conjunctival collagen, producing elastotic degeneration of the stroma and growth of fibrovascular tissue. A pinguecula is a similar yellow, sun-related degeneration of the conjunctiva that does not cross onto the cornea. A pterygium causes irritation and redness; as it advances it flattens the cornea in one meridian, causing astigmatism, and if it reaches the pupil it blocks the visual axis.

The lens is suspended from the ciliary body by zonular fibers, whose main structural protein is fibrillin-1. Ectopia lentis, displacement of the lens, occurs when these fibers are weak or broken, and patients notice blurred or double vision in one eye, large changes in refraction, or a trembling iris (iridodonesis) because the iris loses its support behind it.

In Marfan syndrome, an autosomal dominant mutation in FBN1 produces defective fibrillin-1, so zonules stretch. The lens usually shifts upward and outward (superotemporally), typically in both eyes, and Marfan eyes also tend to be long and myopic, which adds to the risk of retinal detachment. In homocystinuria, usually autosomal recessive cystathionine beta-synthase deficiency, homocysteine accumulates. Zonular fibrillin is rich in cysteine, and excess homocysteine is thought to disrupt its disulfide bonds, so the zonules degrade and break, and the lens tends to fall downward and inward (inferonasally). Homocystinuria also causes a marfanoid habitus, intellectual disability, and arterial and venous thrombosis, which help separate the two diseases.

blocks.title: Ectopia lentis
rows: Aortic root dilation, tall habitus, joint laxity
blocks.caption: Both weaken fibrillin-rich zonules; the direction of displacement differs.

blocks.text: A corneal abrasion is loss of corneal epithelium from a scratch, fingernail, contact lens, or foreign body. Because the cornea is so densely innervated, the patient has severe pain, tearing, photophobia, and a foreign body sensation. Intact epithelium, sealed by tight junctions and covered with lipid-rich membranes, excludes the water-soluble dye fluorescein, but where epithelium is missing the dye enters the stroma and glows green under cobalt blue light, outlining the defect. Vertical linear abrasions suggest a foreign body under the upper lid. An embedded iron fragment leaves a brown rust ring.

Hyphema is blood in the anterior chamber, usually from blunt trauma that tears vessels at the iris root or ciliary body. Red cells settle inferiorly as a level and can block the trabecular meshwork, raising IOP. In sickle cell disease or trait, red cells sickle in the low-oxygen, acidic aqueous, stiffen, and obstruct the meshwork even more readily, so pressure and optic nerve damage occur at lower levels. A subconjunctival hemorrhage, by contrast, is blood beneath the conjunctiva from rupture of a small vessel during coughing, straining, minor trauma, or anticoagulant use. It is bright red, sharply bordered, and painless, vision is normal, and it clears within about 1 to 2 weeks.

An orbital floor (blowout) fracture occurs when a blunt object larger than the orbital opening, such as a fist or ball, strikes the eye. Pressure in the orbit rises suddenly and breaks its thinnest walls, the floor over the maxillary sinus or the medial wall. Orbital fat and the inferior rectus can herniate into the fracture and become trapped, so the eye cannot look up and the patient has vertical double vision. Injury to the infraorbital nerve in its canal numbs the cheek and upper lip, and the globe may sink (enophthalmos). In children a trapdoor fracture can tightly trap the muscle with little visible injury, and traction on it can trigger the oculocardiac reflex (trigeminal afferent, vagal efferent), causing bradycardia, nausea, and vomiting.

Chemical burns differ by agent. Alkalis (lye, ammonia, lime) saponify the lipids of cell membranes, causing liquefactive necrosis that keeps dissolving tissue and lets the alkali penetrate the stroma and anterior chamber. Acids denature and precipitate surface proteins, causing coagulative necrosis that forms a barrier and limits penetration (hydrofluoric acid is an exception). Alkali burns are therefore more severe, and blanching of the limbus means its blood supply and stem cells are destroyed, so the cornea cannot heal normally.

integration.text: Anatomy explains most of the patterns in this chapter. The orbital septum and the thin lamina papyracea separate a harmless lid infection from one that can reach the cavernous sinus, the central retinal artery as an end artery explains the sudden, total loss in CRAO, and the short, horizontal eustachian tube explains why otitis media is a childhood disease. Physiology adds the timing: aqueous outflow resistance, endolymph volume, the tonic balance of the vestibular nerves, and the critical period of the visual cortex each set how fast and in what order symptoms appear.

Biochemistry, microbiology, immunology, and pathology supply the remaining links. Aldose reductase connects diabetes and galactosemia to cataract, fibrillin connects Marfan syndrome and homocystinuria to the lens, and VEGF connects wet AMD, proliferative diabetic retinopathy, and ischemic CRVO. The same organisms recur across sites (Pseudomonas in contact lens keratitis, otitis externa, and perichondritis; S. aureus in hordeolum, cellulitis, and dacryocystitis), and the immune status of the host decides whether CMV causes retinitis and how severe toxoplasmic disease becomes. The limit of pattern recognition is that the red eye, vertigo, and monocular vision loss each have look-alikes, including stroke, so the mechanism behind each sign is what separates them.

summary: A hordeolum is an acute, painful S. aureus gland infection; a chalazion is a painless lipogranuloma from a blocked meibomian gland.
Cataract is light scattering by aggregated or swollen lens proteins; aldose reductase converts glucose and galactose to trapped, osmotically active polyols.

Watery discharge with a preauricular node suggests adenovirus, purulent discharge suggests bacteria (hyperacute with gonococcus), and itching suggests type I allergy; trachoma blinds by tarsal scarring.
Glaucoma is ganglion cell axon loss with disc cupping: open-angle is painless peripheral loss from trabecular resistance, and angle closure is a painful pupillary block emergency.
Pain, reduced vision, an abnormal pupil, or a corneal change mark keratitis, uveitis, or angle closure rather than conjunctivitis.
Dry AMD is drusen and slow atrophy; wet AMD is VEGF-driven choroidal neovascularization with rapid central loss and distortion.
HLA-B27 disease, sarcoidosis, and JIA cause anterior uveitis; Toxoplasma and CMV in AIDS cause posterior uveitis and retinitis.
Vertigo lasting seconds with position is BPPV, hours with low-frequency loss is Meniere disease, and days is vestibular neuritis, or labyrinthitis when hearing is lost.
Eustachian tube obstruction underlies otitis media; Pseudomonas causes otitis externa, malignant otitis externa in diabetics, and perichondritis that spares the lobule.
Weber lateralizes toward conductive loss and away from sensorineural loss; a negative Rinne means conductive loss in that ear.

verify: Percentages and thresholds are approximate and vary among sources: dry AMD about 85 to 90% of cases, cup-to-disc ratio above about 0.6 as suspicious, IOP often above 40 mmHg in acute angle closure, and CMV retinitis at CD4 below 50 cells per microliter.
Meniere vertigo duration of 20 minutes to 12 hours follows the 2015 Barany Society criteria; confirm NABNE uses the same range.
The age at which the critical period for amblyopia closes is commonly given as about 7 to 10 years and is debated; confirm the figure NABNE expects if tested.
Neonatal conjunctivitis timing (gonococcal about 2 to 5 days, chlamydial about 5 to 14 days) varies slightly among sources.
The mechanism of zonular failure in homocystinuria (homocysteine disrupting fibrillin disulfide bonds) is the leading explanation but not fully established.
